name: Scientific Communication
what: This subtopic covers the conventions of scientific communication for VCE Chemistry, including the structure and content of a scientific poster, the use of correct units and significant figures, referencing in Harvard format, and how to write a justified conclusion.
why: The VCE Chemistry School-assessed Coursework requires students to present their investigation as a scientific poster of no more than 600 words. Mastery of these communication conventions is directly assessed and reflects skills used by professional scientists.

items.title: I can describe the structure and key sections of a scientific poster
items.what: A VCE scientific poster includes the following sections in order: title, student name, introduction (including aim and hypothesis), methodology and methods, results, communication statement, discussion, conclusion, and references and acknowledgements.
items.why: The poster template is specified in the VCAA Chemistry Study Design. Students must follow this structure for School-assessed Coursework. The communication statement — a single engaging sentence summarising the key finding — occupies approximately one quarter of the poster.
items.example: A communication statement for the invertase investigation might read: 'The presence of the enzyme invertase increased the rate of glucose production from the hydrolysis of sucrose by a factor of six compared with the uninhibited reaction.' This is a single sentence and would be presented prominently on the poster.

items.title: I can use correct SI units and convert between units used in chemistry
items.what: Quantitative results must be reported with appropriate SI units. Common conversions include: mL to L (divide by 1000), g to kg (divide by 1000), and concentration in mol L^-1 to g L^-1 (multiply by molar mass).
items.why: Incorrect or missing units in calculations and results tables cost marks in VCE assessments. Unit conversions are required for gas law calculations and mole calculations, making this a high-frequency skill.
items.example: To convert 250 mL to litres: 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 L. To convert a concentration of 0.500 mol L^-1 NaOH to g L^-1: 0.500 mol L^-1 × 40.00 g mol^-1 = 20.0 g L^-1.

items.title: I can determine the correct number of significant figures in a value
items.what: Significant figures indicate the precision of a measurement. All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Leading zeros are not significant. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
items.why: Reporting answers to an inappropriate number of significant figures is penalised in VCE. The number of significant figures in an answer should reflect the precision of the least precise measurement used in the calculation.
items.example: 34.980 has 5 significant figures (all digits including trailing zero after decimal). 10.0 has 3 significant figures (the trailing zero after the decimal is significant). 0.0034 has 2 significant figures (leading zeros are not significant, only the 3 and 4 are).

items.title: I can write a justified conclusion that evaluates evidence against a hypothesis
items.what: A conclusion briefly states the key finding of the investigation with reference to specific data, assesses whether the results support or do not support the hypothesis, and avoids introducing new information not discussed in the results and discussion. Terms such as 'supported' and 'indicated' are used rather than 'proved' or 'disproved'.
items.why: A conclusion is not simply a restatement of results. It must make a claim about what the data means in relation to the hypothesis and the broader chemistry. Using 'proved' implies absolute certainty, which is not appropriate for a single investigation.
items.example: Correct conclusion language: 'The results indicate that the presence of invertase increased the rate of hydrolysis of sucrose, with glucose concentration reaching 20.0 mg mL^-1 at 180 s compared with 3.00 mg mL^-1 in the absence of invertase. These results support the hypothesis.'

items.title: I can reference a source correctly using Harvard format
items.what: Harvard referencing requires four elements for most sources: author surname and initials, year of publication in brackets, title, and source details. References are listed in alphabetical order by author surname. Websites must include the URL and the date accessed.
items.why: Correct referencing is required in the poster to avoid plagiarism and to allow readers to locate the original sources. VCE assessment rubrics include marks for correct referencing format.
items.example: Book reference: Drummond, B., Maaser, S., Angley, L., Greaves, R., Fraser, S., Lucas, T., and Wang, Z. (2023). Cambridge Chemistry VCE Units 1 and 2. Cambridge University Press. Website reference: United Nations. (2022). The 17 goals | Sustainable development. https://sdgs.un.org/goals, accessed 27 October 2023.

items.title: I can interpret investigation outcomes in terms of broader chemical concepts
items.what: Interpreting outcomes means connecting the results of the investigation to the underlying chemical theory — for example, explaining how collision theory accounts for observed rate changes, or how enzyme mechanism explains the plateau in product concentration.
items.why: Results without chemical explanation demonstrate data recording but not scientific understanding. VCE rubrics reward students who can link experimental observations to relevant chemical models and theories.
items.example: In the invertase investigation, if glucose concentration plateaus at 20.0 mg mL^-1 after 180 s, a student can interpret this by noting that the substrate (sucrose) has been fully consumed, so no further hydrolysis can occur regardless of invertase concentration remaining.
